claim: Typhoid toxin is a virulence factor for the bacterial pathogen Salmonella Typhi, which causes typhoid fever in humans.
source: Typhoid toxin is a virulence factor for the bacterial pathogen Salmonella Typhi, which causes typhoid fever in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Galán, 2016; Parry et al., 2002; Crump and Mintz, 2010; Raffatellu et al., 2008; Wain et al., 2015; Dougan and Baker, 2014).

claim: After its synthesis by intracellular bacteria, typhoid toxin is secreted into the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole.
source: After its synthesis by intracellular bacteria, typhoid toxin is secreted into the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole by a secretion mechanism strictly dependent on TtsA, a specific muramidase that facilitates toxin transport through the peptidoglycan layer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Spanò et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2019).

claim: Typhoid toxin secretion is strictly dependent on TtsA, a specific muramidase that facilitates toxin transport through the peptidoglycan layer.
source: After its synthesis by intracellular bacteria, typhoid toxin is secreted into the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole by a secretion mechanism strictly dependent on TtsA, a specific muramidase that facilitates toxin transport through the peptidoglycan layer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Hodak and Galán, 2013; Geiger et al., 2018).

claim: Substrate recognition by TtsA depends on a discrete domain within its carboxy terminus.
source: Here we show that substrate recognition by TtsA depends on a discrete domain within its carboxy terminus, which targets the enzyme to the bacterial poles to recognize YcbB-edited peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The carboxy-terminal domain of TtsA targets the enzyme to the bacterial poles to recognize YcbB-edited peptidoglycan.
source: Here we show that substrate recognition by TtsA depends on a discrete domain within its carboxy terminus, which targets the enzyme to the bacterial poles to recognize YcbB-edited peptidoglycan.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Typhoid toxin is only produced by intracellular bacteria.
source: This toxin is unique in that is only produced by intracellular bacteria (Haghjoo and Galán, 2004; Fowler and Galán, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: After synthesis, typhoid toxin is secreted into the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole, packaged into vesicle carriers, and subsequently transported to the extracellular environment.
source: After its synthesis, the toxin is secreted into the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole, packaged into vesicle carriers, and subsequently transported to the extracellular environment from where it can reach its target cells (Spanò et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Typhoid toxin secretion from the bacterial cell is mediated by a unique transport mechanism that requires the activity of TtsA.
source: Typhoid toxin secretion from the bacterial cell is mediated by a unique transport mechanism that requires the activity of TtsA, a specialized muramidase that facilitates the translocation of typhoid toxin from the cis to the trans side of the peptidoglycan (PG) layer of the bacterial envelope (Hodak and Galán, 2013; Geiger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The bacterial peptidoglycan is composed of glycan strands made up of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNac) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNac) linked by β-(1, 4) glycosidic bonds.
source: The bacterial PG is composed of glycan strands made up of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNac) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNac) linked by β-(1, 4) glycosidic bonds (Turner et al., 2014; Egan et al., 2015; Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations describing established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure.

claim: Peptidoglycan glycan strands are connected by short peptides composed of L- and D-amino acids, which are cross-linked to one another by specific transpeptidases.
source: These strands are connected by short peptides composed of L- and D-amino acids, which are cross-linked to one another by specific transpeptidases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure.

claim: Most peptidoglycan cross-links are between the carboxyl group of D-Ala at position 4 of one peptide to the ε-amino group of the m-Dap residue at position 3 of another (D-D cross-links).
source: Most of these cross-links are between the carboxyl group of D-Ala at position 4 of one peptide to the ε-amino group of the m-Dap residue at position 3 of another (D-D cross-links) (Glauner et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Peptidoglycan crosslinks can also occur between two m-Dap residues of adjacent stem peptides (L-D cross-links), although these are less abundant.
source: However, although less abundant, crosslinks can also occur between two m-Dap residues of adjacent stem peptides (L-D cross-links) (Glauner et al., 1988; Höltje, 1998; Quintela et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: TtsA exerts its function at the bacterial poles.
source: In previous studies we have shown that TtsA is unique in that it exerts its function at the bacterial poles, and it requires the activity of YcbB, a bacterial transpeptidase that is responsible for introducing L-D crosslinks to the peptides that link the glycan strands of the peptidoglycan layer (Geiger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TtsA requires the activity of YcbB, a bacterial transpeptidase that is responsible for introducing L-D crosslinks to the peptides that link the glycan strands of the peptidoglycan layer.
source: In previous studies we have shown that TtsA is unique in that it exerts its function at the bacterial poles, and it requires the activity of YcbB, a bacterial transpeptidase that is responsible for introducing L-D crosslinks to the peptides that link the glycan strands of the peptidoglycan layer (Geiger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TtsA-mediated PG remodeling and typhoid toxin secretion occurs exclusively at the bacterial poles.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, TtsA-mediated PG remodeling and typhoid toxin secretion occurs exclusively at the bacterial poles (Geiger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sen1395, a close TtsA homolog encoded by Salmonella Enteritidis, was unable to complement a S. Typhi ∆ttsA mutant strain for its ability to form typhoid-toxin vesicle carriers in infected cells.
source: We have previously shown that Sen1395, a close TtsA homolog encoded by Salmonella Enteritidis (Figure 1a), was unable to complement a S. Typhi ∆ttsA mutant strain for its ability to form typhoid-toxin vesicle carriers in infected cells (Hodak and Galán, 2013), an indirect measure of typhoid toxin in vivo secretion from the bacterial cell (Spanò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When ttsA was replaced with sen1395 in the S. Typhi chromosome, the resulting strain was unable to mediate the translocation of typhoid toxin from the cis to the trans side of the PG layer.
source: Consistent with this observation we found that, when we replaced ttsA in the S. Typhi chromosome with sen1395, the resulting strain was unable to mediate the translocation of typhoid toxin from the cis to the trans side of the PG layer (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A chimera made up of the amino terminal half of Sen1395 (amino acids 1–92) and the carboxy-terminal half of TtsA (amino acids 93–180) was able to fully complement ∆ttsA S. Typhi mutant strain for the translocation of typhoid toxin across the PG layer.
source: We found that a chimera made up of the amino terminal half of Sen1395 (amino acids 1–92), which contains its catalytic domain, and the carboxy-terminal half of TtsA (amino acids 93–180) was able to fully complement ∆ttsA S. Typhi mutant strain for the translocation of typhoid toxin across the PG layer (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The substrate-binding and protein secretion specific functions of TtsA are contained within its carboxy terminal domain.
source: These findings support the notion that the substrate-binding and protein secretion specific functions of TtsA are contained within its carboxy terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the chimera experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Differences in substrate-recognition rather than substrate catalysis are responsible for Sen1395's inability to mediate typhoid toxin secretion.
source: More broadly, the observation that Sen1395 cannot complement a ∆ttsA S. Typhi mutant for typhoid toxin secretion but that its catalytic domain can be exchanged with TtsA's without affecting protein secretion function suggests that differences in substrate-recognition rather than substrate catalysis are responsible for Sen1395's inability to mediate typhoid toxin secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the chimera experiments.

claim: Overexpression of full-length TtsA in wild-type S. Typhi halted its growth due to PG hydrolysis.
source: Consequently, over-expression of full-length TtsA in wild-type S. Typhi halted its growth (due to PG hydrolysis), but its overexpression in the ∆ycbB S. Typhi mutant did not (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Overexpression of TtsA in the ∆ycbB S. Typhi mutant did not halt bacterial growth.
source: Consequently, over-expression of full-length TtsA in wild-type S. Typhi halted its growth (due to PG hydrolysis), but its overexpression in the ∆ycbB S. Typhi mutant did not (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Overexpression of a chimeric construct consisting of the amino-terminal catalytic domain (1-92) of Sen1395 and the carboxy-terminal substrate binding domain (93-180) of TtsA was able to halt the growth of wild-type S. Typhi but not the growth of the ∆ycbB mutant strain.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that the carboxy-terminus of TtsA confers its substrate specificity, over expression of a chimeric construct consisting of the amino-terminal catalytic domain (1-92) of Sen1395 and the carboxy-terminal substrate binding domain (93-180) of TtsA was able to halt the growth of wild-type S. Typhi but not the growth of the ∆ycbB mutant strain (Figure 1c) despite equivalent levels of expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Overexpression of full-length Sen1395 was able to halt the growth of both wild type and the ∆ycbB mutant strains.
source: In contrast, overexpression of full-length Sen1395 was able to halt the growth of both wild type and the ∆ycbB mutant strains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The proportion of LD crosslinks increases significantly when bacteria are grown in TTIM.
source: We have previously shown that the proportion of LD crosslinks increases significantly when bacteria are grown in TTIM (Geiger et al., 2018), a culture medium that mimics conditions found by intracellular Salmonella.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Purified TtsA is not able to hydrolyze PG isolated from LB grown bacteria.
source: Consequently, while purified TtsA is not able to hydrolyze PG isolated from LB grown bacteria, it is able to effectively hydrolyze PG obtained after S. Typhi growth in TTIM (Geiger et al., 2018) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and a citation to previous work.

claim: Purified TtsA is able to effectively hydrolyze PG obtained after S. Typhi growth in TTIM.
source: Consequently, while purified TtsA is not able to hydrolyze PG isolated from LB grown bacteria, it is able to effectively hydrolyze PG obtained after S. Typhi growth in TTIM (Geiger et al., 2018) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and a citation to previous work.

claim: Purified Sen1395 was able to hydrolyze PG isolated from both wild type and ∆ycbB S. Typhi, after growth in LB or TTIM.
source: We found that purified Sen1395 was able to hydrolyze PG isolated from both wild type and ∆ycbB S. Typhi, after growth in LB or TTIM, although the latter to a lesser extent (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Purified Sen1395 was unable to hydrolyze PG isolated from a strain overproducing YcbB and thus containing an increased proportion of LD cross-links.
source: However, purified Sen1395 was unable to hydrolyze PG isolated from a strain overproducing YcbB and thus containing an increased proportion of LD cross-links (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Sen1395 and TtsA exhibit different PG specificity.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Sen1395 and TtsA exhibit different PG specificity and that the substrate specificity determinants of both TtsA and Sen1395 are contained within their carboxy-terminal half.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The substrate specificity determinants of both TtsA and Sen1395 are contained within their carboxy-terminal half.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Sen1395 and TtsA exhibit different PG specificity and that the substrate specificity determinants of both TtsA and Sen1395 are contained within their carboxy-terminal half.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Unlike TtsA, when expressed in S. Typhi Sen1395 was not enriched at the poles and showed a uniformed distribution around the bacterial surface.
source: We found that, unlike TtsA, when expressed in S. Typhi Sen1395 was not enriched at the poles and showed a uniformed distribution around the bacterial surface (Figure 2a and b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a, 2b, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TtsA carboxy-terminus is essential for polar localization.
source: We found that the TtsA carboxy-terminus is essential for polar localization since a chimera consisting of the first 92 amino acids of Sen1395 and amino acids 93 to 180 of TtsA localized to the pole (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There is a strict correlation between the ability of TtsA/Sen1395 chimeric constructs to complement a S. Typhi ∆ttsA mutant for typhoid toxin PG translocation and their polar localization.
source: Furthermore, we found a strict correlation between the ability of these constructs to complement a S. Typhi ∆ttsA mutant for typhoid toxin PG translocation (Figure 1b) and their polar localization (Figure 2a and c), supporting the notion that polar localization is essential for TtsA protein secretion function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Polar localization is essential for TtsA protein secretion function.
source: Furthermore, we found a strict correlation between the ability of these constructs to complement a S. Typhi ∆ttsA mutant for typhoid toxin PG translocation (Figure 1b) and their polar localization (Figure 2a and c), supporting the notion that polar localization is essential for TtsA protein secretion function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Expression of chimeric constructs containing the carboxy-terminus of TtsA and therefore targeted to the bacterial poles, strictly correlated with the presence of PG remodeling at these sites.
source: We found that expression of the chimeric constructs containing the carboxy-terminus of TtsA and therefore targeted to the bacterial poles, strictly correlated with the presence of PG remodeling at these sites (Figure 2c and d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c, 2d, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The polar localization of TtsA in the ∆ycbB mutant was indistinguishable from wild type.
source: However, we found that the polar localization of TtsA in the ∆ycbB mutant was indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 2a and d) indicating that the presence of L-D-crosslinked PG per se is not essential for the polar localization of TtsA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and 2d.

claim: The presence of L-D-crosslinked PG per se is not essential for the polar localization of TtsA.
source: However, we found that the polar localization of TtsA in the ∆ycbB mutant was indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 2a and d) indicating that the presence of L-D-crosslinked PG per se is not essential for the polar localization of TtsA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Changing asparagine at position 166 of TtsA to aspartic acid (N166D) impaired the formation of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates in S. Typhi infected cells.
source: We have previously shown that changing asparagine at position 166 of TtsA to aspartic acid (N166D), which is the residue present in Sen1395 at the equivalent position, impaired the formation of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates in S. Typhi infected cells, an indirect measurement of toxin secretion (Hodak and Galán, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The TtsA N166D mutation severely impeded TtsA-mediated typhoid toxin translocation across the PG layer.
source: Consistent with these findings we found that this mutation severely impeded TtsA-mediated typhoid toxin translocation across the PG layer (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Introduction of an asparagine at position 166 in Sen1395 (D166N) conferred on this protein homolog the ability to partially complement typhoid toxin translocation across the PG in a ∆ttsA S. Typhi mutant strain.
source: Conversely, introduction of an asparagine at the same position in Sen1395 (D166N) conferred on this protein homolog the ability to partially complement typhoid toxin translocation across the PG in a ∆ttsA S. Typhi mutant strain (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TtsA N166 plays an important role in conferring on this muramidase the ability to translocate typhoid toxin across the PG layer.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that TtsA N166 plays an important role in conferring on this muramidase the ability to translocate typhoid toxin across the PG layer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: TtsAN166D localized to the bacterial poles in a manner indistinguishable from wild type.
source: We found that this mutant localized to the bacterial poles in a manner indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 3b and c) suggesting that N166 is not essential for polar localization but rather, it may be involved in the recognition of L-D-cross-linked PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: N166 is not essential for polar localization but rather, it may be involved in the recognition of L-D-cross-linked PG.
source: We found that this mutant localized to the bacterial poles in a manner indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 3b and c) suggesting that N166 is not essential for polar localization but rather, it may be involved in the recognition of L-D-cross-linked PG.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Expression of TtsAN166D did not lead to PG remodeling at the bacterial poles.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, expression of TtsAN166D did not lead to PG remodeling at the bacterial poles (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and 3e.

claim: Introduction of the critical asparagine at an equivalent position in Sen1395 (Sen1395D167N) resulted in its partially relocalization to the bacterial poles.
source: However, introduction of this critical asparagine at an equivalent position in Sen1395 (Sen1395D167N) resulted in its partially relocalization to the bacterial poles suggesting a complex role for this residue in both substrate recognition and polar localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Polar localization and substrate recognition are functionally separable activities that are mediated by different TtsA determinants.
source: Taken together, these results implicate a role for the carboxy-terminal domain of TtsA in its polar localization and suggest that polar localization and substrate recognition are functionally separable activities that are mediated by different TtsA determinants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The TtsA structure shows two defined globular α-helical domains separated by a 'hinge' that is formed by a bent α-helix.
source: The TtsA structure shows two defined globular α-helical domains separated by a 'hinge' that is formed by a bent α-helix (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The amino terminal domain of TtsA (amino acids 1 to 64) contains the lysozyme-like catalytic triad (Glu14, Asp19, Thr28).
source: The amino terminal domain (amino acids 1 to 64) contains the lysozyme-like catalytic triad (Glu14, Asp19, Thr28) situated under a 'flap' formed by a loop that is anchored to the domain by interactions with three short helixes (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The carboxy-terminal substrate-binding domain of TtsA (amino acids 68 to 180) is composed of 6 anti parallel α-helices that organize into a helix bundle.
source: The carboxy-terminal substrate-binding domain (amino acids 68 to 180) is composed of 6 anti parallel α-helices that organize into a helix bundle (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The helix bundle of the carboxy-terminal domain serves as a support for a platform with a central groove, which together with the catalytic triad-containing flap forms a ring-like structure.
source: The helix bundle serves as a support for a platform with a central groove, which together with the catalytic triad-containing flap forms a ring-like structure (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The ring-like structure formed by the central groove and catalytic flap is proposed to be the site of engagement of the peptidoglycan substrate.
source: As will be elaborated below, this ring-like structure is proposed to be the site of engagement of the peptidoglycan substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a hypothesis based on the structural data.

claim: TtsA shares structural similarity with NMB1012 from Neisseria meningitides (PDB 2is5) and PG_0293 from Porphyromonas gingivalis (PDB 2nr7).
source: However, two of the structures, NMB1012 from Neisseria meningitides (PDB 2is5) and PG_0293 from Porphyromonas gingivalis (PDB 2nr7)) shared stronger structural similarity than the others (z scores of 13 and 9.5, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison using Dali search.

claim: TtsA has 27% sequence identity with NMB1012 and a root-mean-square deviation (rmsd) of 1.3 Å over 70 aligned Cα pairs.
source: TtsA has 27% sequence identity with NMB1012 and a root-mean-square deviation (rmsd) of 1.3 Å over 70 aligned Cα pairs, and has 15% sequence identity with PG_0293 and rmsd of 1.0 Å over 34 aligned Cα pairs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison.

claim: TtsA has 15% sequence identity with PG_0293 and rmsd of 1.0 Å over 34 aligned Cα pairs.
source: TtsA has 27% sequence identity with NMB1012 and a root-mean-square deviation (rmsd) of 1.3 Å over 70 aligned Cα pairs, and has 15% sequence identity with PG_0293 and rmsd of 1.0 Å over 34 aligned Cα pairs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison.

claim: The catalytic domain of Neisseria meningitides NMB1012 aligns well with that of TtsA, and the predicted catalytic residues overlap well in the two structures.
source: The catalytic domain of Neisseria meningitides NMB1012 also aligns well with that of TtsA. In particular, the predicted catalytic residues overlap well in the two structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In PG_0293, the flap containing the catalytic residues is translocated 90 degrees to the side, placing it away from the proposed substrate-binding site.
source: However, in the case of PG_0293, the flap containing the catalytic residues is translocated 90 degrees to the side, placing it away from the proposed substrate-binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Electron density not corresponding to protein residues was identified in all four independent TtsA copies in the crystal at one of the ends of the substrate-binding groove.
source: Electron density not corresponding to protein residues was identified in all four independent TtsA copies in the crystal at one of the ends of what we propose to be the substrate-binding groove of TtsA (see below) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Diaminopimelic acid (API) could be modeled into the electron density with an optimal fit indicating that this density corresponds to the muropeptide stem (or a portion of it) of an E. coli peptidoglycan fragment presumably bound to TtsA after lysis and carried through the purification procedure.
source: Diaminopimelic acid (API) could be modeled into this density with an optimal fit indicating that this density corresponds to the muropeptide stem (or a portion of it) of an E. coli peptidoglycan fragment presumably bound to TtsA after lysis and carried through the purification procedure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on analysis of the crystal structure and modeling.

claim: The API ligand sits within a cavity and is stabilized by hydrogen bond contacts between the NH2 group of API and D118 in TtsA, and the COOH group of API and T125.
source: The ligand itself sits within a cavity and it is stabilized by hydrogen bond contacts between the NH2 group of API and D118 in TtsA, and the COOH group of API and T125 (Figure 4d and (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: S. Typhi expressing TtsAD118A, TtsAI116D, or TtsAN166D were unable to translocate typhoid toxin indicating that these residues play a critical role in substrate recognition.
source: We found that S. Typhi expressing TtsAD118A, TtsAI116D, or TtsAN166D were unable to translocate typhoid toxin indicating that these residues play a critical role in substrate recognition (Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Comparison of the structures of the different molecules within the TtsA asymmetric unit revealed two different conformations, one shared by chains A, B, and D, and another in chain C.
source: Comparison of the structures of the different molecules within the TtsA asymmetric unit revealed two different conformations, one conformation shared by chains A, B, and D, and another conformation in chain C.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The two alternative conformations of TtsA position the flap that contains the catalytic residues either closer or further apart (~6.1 Å) from the substrate-binding groove, resulting in either a close or open ring-like structure.
source: These two alternative conformations, while overall largely identical, position the flap that contains the catalytic residues either closer or further apart (~6.1 Å) from the substrate-binding groove, resulting in either a close or open ring-like structure (Figure 4f and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4f and Video 1.

claim: The repositioning of the catalytic site in the two TtsA conformations is the consequence of discrete conformational changes in the hinge that separates the amino terminal (catalytic) and carboxy-terminal (substrate-binding) domains.
source: The repositioning of the catalytic site in these two configurations is the consequence of discrete conformational changes in the hinge that separates the amino terminal (catalytic) and carboxy-terminal (substrate-binding) domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The two alternative conformations of TtsA may represent alternative conformations adopted by TtsA during catalysis.
source: Although the functional relevance of these two conformations is unknown, it is possible that they represent alternative conformations adopted by TtsA during catalysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is speculation based on the structural data.

claim: The TtsA structure aligns very well to Sen1395 with an rmsd of ~0.7 Å over 161 aligned Cα pairs (with 64% sequence identity).
source: The structure aligns very well to TtsA with an rmsd of ~0.7 Å over 161 aligned Cα pairs (with 64% sequence identity) (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The positions of the conserved catalytic residues in TtsA and Sen1395 overlap reasonably well.
source: The positions of the conserved catalytic residues in both enzymes overlap reasonably well, which is consistent with the observation that the catalytic domain of TtsA can be replaced with the catalytic domain of Sen1395 and retain full function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison.

claim: Despite the very high structural similarity of TtsA and Sen1395, notable differences on amino acids located on the surface of the putative substrate-biding groove could be identified.
source: Despite the very high structural similarity of the two enzymes, notable differences on amino acids located on the surface of the putative substrate-biding groove could be identified (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The surface of the substrate-binding groove in TtsA is lined by largely uncharged amino acids (Ile116, Gln120, Gln164, Asn166), while the equivalent surface in Sen1395 is occupied by several charged amino acids (Asp117, Arg121, Glu165, Asp167).
source: Notably, while the surface of the substrate-binding groove in TtsA is lined by largely uncharged amino acids (Ile116, Gln120, Gln164, Asn166), the equivalent surface in Sen1395 is occupied by several charged amino acids (Asp117, Arg121, Glu165, Asp167).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison.

claim: The charge differences in the substrate-binding domain between TtsA and Sen1395 confer upon these enzymes their different substrate specificity.
source: We propose that the charge differences in the substrate-binding domain between TtsA and Sen1395 confer upon these enzymes their different substrate specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a hypothesis based on the structural comparison.

claim: After UV treatment, TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA were no longer detectable by western blot, although TtsAE14pBpA was detectable at equal levels than those prior to UV exposure.
source: However, after exposure to UV light, TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA were no longer detectable by western blot, although TtsAE14pBpA was detectable at equal levels than those prior to UV exposure (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The inability to detect TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA after UV exposure was due to their crosslinking to the peptide stem of the PG polymer, which because of its high molecular weight prevented their migration into SDS-PAGE gels.
source: We hypothesized that the inability to detect these TtsA constructs was due to their crosslinking to the peptide stem of the PG polymer, which because of its high molecular weight prevented their migration into SDS-PAGE gels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: After treatment with lysozyme, TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA were readily detectable at equal levels than TtsAE14pBpA indicating that these mutant constructs were crosslinked to PG after UV treatment.
source: We found that after treatment with lysozyme we were able to readily detect TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA at equal levels than TtsAE14pBpA Indicating that these mutant constructs were crosslinked to PG after UV treatment (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: After lysozyme treatment, TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA were detected as two bands: one migrating as ~25 kDa polypeptide (predicted size of a TtsA monomer), and another migrating as a 50 kDa polypeptide (consistent with the size of a TtsA dimer).
source: Interestingly, in the case of TtsAD118pBpA, TtsAN166pBpA and TtsAF169pBpA we detected two bands after lysozyme treatment: one migrating as ~25 kDa polypeptide, the predicted size of a TtsA monomer, and another migrating as a 50 kDa polypeptide, consistent with the size of a TtsA dimer (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TtsA behaves as a monomer in solution.
source: Since TtsA behaves as a monomer in solution, the dimer is unlikely to be the result of TtsA/TtsA crosslinks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on size exclusion chromatography data mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The TtsA dimer detected after UV crosslinking and lysozyme treatment is unlikely to be the result of TtsA/TtsA crosslinks, but rather TtsA monomers must bind two adjacent cross-linked muropeptides.
source: Since TtsA behaves as a monomer in solution, the dimer is unlikely to be the result of TtsA/TtsA crosslinks. Furthermore, the location of the labeled amino acids in the predicted substrate-binding groove within the TtsA structure dictates that it is unlikely that this region could engage into putative TtsA-TtsA interactions. Rather, these results suggest that TtsA must bind two adjacent cross-linked muropeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the experimental data and structural analysis.

claim: Only monomers (with or without lysozyme treatment) were detected when the UV crosslinking experiment was conducted in a S. Typhi ∆ycbB strain, which lacks LD-crosslinked PG.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, only monomers (with or without lysozyme treatment) were detected when the experiment was conducted in a S. Typhi ∆ycbB strain, which lacks LD-crosslinked PG and therefore it is not permissive for TtsA activity (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Addition of the crosslinker BS3 to purified TtsA did not result in the formation of a dimer.
source: Consistent with our observation that purified TtsA behaves as a monomer in solution, addition of the crosslinker to purified TtsA did not result in the formation of a dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on in vitro crosslinking experiments.

claim: Addition of the crosslinker BS3 to purified TtsA in the presence of purified peptidoglycan resulted in the formation of a TtsA species that migrated at ~50 kDa.
source: In contrast, addition of the crosslinker to purified TtsA in the presence of purified peptidoglycan resulted in the formation of a TtsA species that migrated at ~50 kDa.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The finding of a substantial proportion of crosslinked dimeric TtsA is consistent with the notion that two TtsA molecules preferably bind two adjacent, cross-linked muropeptides.
source: Since the efficiency of both the in vitro and in vivo crosslinking reactions is expected to be much less than 100%, the finding of a substantial proportion of crosslinked dimeric TtsA is consistent with the notion that two TtsA molecules preferably bind two adjacent, cross-linked muropeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the crosslinking experimental data.

claim: The secretion of typhoid toxin is dependent on a unique protein secretion mechanism specifically adapted for the biology of the intracellular pathogen S. Typhi.
source: The secretion of typhoid toxin is dependent on a unique protein secretion mechanism specifically adapted for the biology of the intracellular pathogen S. Typhi (Geiger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: In the typhoid toxin secretion mechanism, the typhoid toxin subunits, PltA, PltB, and CdtB, are first secreted to the periplasmic space by the sec translocation machinery through the engagement of canonical secretion signals in each one of these polypeptides.
source: In this secretion mechanism, the typhoid toxin subunits, PltA, PltB, and CdtB, are first secreted to the periplasmic space by the sec translocation machinery through the engagement of canonical secretion signals in each one of these polypeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge about the typhoid toxin secretion pathway.

claim: Once in the periplasm, the typhoid toxin protein subunits are assembled into the holotoxin complex, which is subsequently translocated to the trans side of the PG layer.
source: Once in the periplasm, the protein subunits are assembled into the holotoxin complex, which is subsequently translocated to the trans side of the PG layer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge about the typhoid toxin secretion pathway.

claim: The holotoxin is released to the outside after exposure to membrane-active compounds such as antimicrobial peptides or bile salts, which are encountered by the bacteria during infection and can introduce minor disruptions to the outer membrane.
source: From this location, the holotoxin is finally released to the outside after exposure to membrane-active compounds such as antimicrobial peptides or bile salts, which are encountered by the bacteria during infection and can introduce minor disruptions to the outer membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge about the typhoid toxin secretion pathway.

claim: The critical step of toxin translocation through the PG layer occurs at the bacterial poles and is mediated by TtsA.
source: The critical step of toxin translocation through the PG layer occurs at the bacterial poles and is mediated by TtsA, which belongs to a unique family of muramidases most often associated with bacteriophage release (Hodak and Galán, 2013; Stojković and Rothman-Denes, 2007; Pei and Grishin, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: TtsA belongs to a unique family of muramidases most often associated with bacteriophage release.
source: The critical step of toxin translocation through the PG layer occurs at the bacterial poles and is mediated by TtsA, which belongs to a unique family of muramidases most often associated with bacteriophage release (Hodak and Galán, 2013; Stojković and Rothman-Denes, 2007; Pei and Grishin, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Unlike its bacteriophage homologs, TtsA exhibits exquisite sensitivity for L-D-crosslinked PG.
source: Unlike its bacteriophage homologs, however, TtsA exhibits exquisite sensitivity for L-D-crosslinked PG, which in most Gram-negative bacteria are less abundant than the most commonly found D-D crosslinked species.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the findings of this study.

claim: By constructing chimeras with the S. Enteritidis Sen1395 protein, the substrate specificity and subcellular localization determinants were mapped to the carboxy terminal domain of TtsA.
source: By constructing chimeras with the S. Enteritidis Sen1395 protein, a close homolog of TtsA with different specificity and subcellular localization, we were able to map the substrate specificity and subcellular localization determinants to its carboxy terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the findings from the chimera experiments.

claim: TtsA also localized to the poles of a S. Typhi ∆ycbB mutant, which lacks L-D crosslinked PG, although with reduced efficiency.
source: However, we found that TtsA also localized to the poles of a S. Typhi ∆ycbB mutant, which lacks L-D crosslinked PG, although with reduced efficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the findings from the localization experiments.

claim: Polar localization can occur without L-D crosslinked PG modification and other determinants must contribute to the targeting of TtsA to this subcellular location.
source: These observations suggest that polar localization can occur without this PG modification and that other determinants must contribute to the targeting of TtsA to this subcellular location.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The mechanisms of polar localization and L-D PG targeting are functionally distinct.
source: These results also indicate that the mechanisms of polar localization and L-D PG targeting are functionally distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: TtsA is organized in two independent domains: an amino-terminal catalytic domain and a carboxy-terminal substrate-binding domain, separated by a bent helix that forms a hinge between these two domains.
source: Entirely consistent with the chimera studies, we found that TtsA is organized in two independent domains: an amino-terminal catalytic domain and a carboxy-terminal substrate-binding domain, separated by a bent helix that forms a hinge between these two domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the structural findings.

claim: The conserved, lysozyme-like catalytic triad is located within a loop that is supported by three short helixes.
source: The conserved, lysozyme-like catalytic triad is located within a loop that is supported by three short helixes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the structural findings.

claim: The catalytic loop reaches out to the substrate-binding groove and in doing so forms a ring-like structure that presumably envelopes the PG and positions the catalytic residues for the cleavage of the PG backbone.
source: This loop reaches out to the substrate-binding groove and in doing so forms a ring-like structure that presumably envelopes the PG and positions the catalytic residues for the cleavage of the PG backbone.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The carboxy-terminal domain contains a helix bundle that forms a platform with a central groove that serves as a binding site for the muropeptide stem.
source: The carboxy-terminal domain contains a helix bundle that forms a platform with a central groove that we postulate serves as a binding site for the muropeptide stem.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on the structural data.

claim: Electron density corresponding to diaminopimelic acid was observed bound to a crevice on one of the ends of the substrate-binding groove.
source: In support of this conclusion, we observed electron density corresponding to diaminopimelic acid bound to a crevice on one of the ends of the substrate-binding groove.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the structural findings.

claim: Mutations in the residue that coordinates the binding to diaminopimelic acid resulted in complete loss of function.
source: Mutations in the residue that coordinates the binding to diaminopimelic acid resulted in complete loss of function, consistent with the notion that this residue plays an essential role in substrate recognition.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the mutagenesis findings.

claim: Comparison of the TtsA and Sen1395 atomic structures revealed specific differences in critical amino acids lining the substrate-binding groove, which result in defined charge differences lining the substrate-binding groove.
source: Comparison of the TtsA and Sen1395 atomic structures revealed specific differences in critical amino acids lining the substrate-binding groove, which result in defined charge differences lining the substrate-binding groove.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the structural comparison findings.

claim: The charge differences in the substrate-binding groove are responsible for the differences in substrate specificity between TtsA and Sen1395.
source: We postulate that these charge differences are responsible for the differences in substrate specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on the structural comparison.

claim: Mutants containing pBpa at positions D118, N166, and F169 cross-linked to PG after exposure to UV light.
source: We found that mutants containing pBpa at positions D118, N166, and F169 cross-linked to PG after exposure to UV light.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the photocrosslinking findings.

claim: A significant proportion of the TtsA cross-linked species migrated in SDS-PAGE as dimers.
source: Interestingly, a significant proportion of the TtsA cross-linked species migrated in SDS-PAGE as dimers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the photocrosslinking findings.

claim: The two TtsA monomers in the dimer must be held together by cross-linked PG species rather than by direct TtsA-TtsA crosslinks.
source: TtsA does not form dimers in solution therefore we interpret these observations to mean that the two monomers must be held together by cross-linked PG species rather than by direct TtsA-TtsA crosslinks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is an interpretation of the crosslinking data.

claim: The TtsA monomers must be cross-linked to adjacent peptide stems of the PG polymer.
source: As the TtsA dimers resisted lysozyme treatment, we hypothesize that the TtsA monomers must be cross-linked to adjacent peptide stems of the PG polymer (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is a hypothesis based on the crosslinking data.

claim: These peptide stems must be the subject of complex crosslinking patterns since lysozyme-treated PG with canonical LD-crosslinks should yield unlinked monomers.
source: These peptide stems must be the subject of complex crosslinking patterns since lysozyme-treated PG with canonical LD-crosslinks should yield unlinked monomers, which in turn would be incompatible with the observed TtsA dimers after UV exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is an inference based on the crosslinking data and knowledge of PG structure.

claim: LD transpeptidation does not require de novo incorporation of new peptidoglycan precursors.
source: LD transpeptidation does not require de novo incorporation of new peptidoglycan precursors, therefore it has been observed that the proportion of LD-crosslinked peptide increases in stationary phase (Turner et al., 2014; de Pedro and Cava, 2015; Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The proportion of LD-crosslinked peptide increases in stationary phase.
source: LD transpeptidation does not require de novo incorporation of new peptidoglycan precursors, therefore it has been observed that the proportion of LD-crosslinked peptide increases in stationary phase (Turner et al., 2014; de Pedro and Cava, 2015; Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: YcbB localizes to the bacterial poles.
source: We have shown that the only LD-transpeptidase in S. Typhi, YcbB, localizes to the bacterial poles so it is possible that the presence of this enzyme at that location may result in the accumulation of cross-linked trimers and tetramers that may be selectively targeted by TtsA (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on findings from this study.

claim: The presence of YcbB at the bacterial poles may result in the accumulation of cross-linked trimers and tetramers that may be selectively targeted by TtsA.
source: We have shown that the only LD-transpeptidase in S. Typhi, YcbB, localizes to the bacterial poles so it is possible that the presence of this enzyme at that location may result in the accumulation of cross-linked trimers and tetramers that may be selectively targeted by TtsA (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is speculation based on the findings.

claim: The accumulation of cross-linked trimers and tetramers at the bacterial poles may provide a mechanism to restrict the enzymatic activity of TtsA to the bacterial poles.
source: This in turn may provide a mechanism to restrict the enzymatic activity of TtsA to the bacterial poles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Comparison of the structures of the four independent molecules in the TtsA crystal revealed the presence of two conformations: an open conformation in which the loop containing the catalytic residues is moved away from the substrate, and a close conformation with the loop in much closer proximity to the substrate-binding groove.
source: Comparison of the structures of the four independent molecules in the TtsA crystal revealed the presence of two conformations: an open conformation in which the loop containing the catalytic residues is moved away from the substrate, and a close conformation with the loop in much closer proximity to the substrate-binding groove.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the structural findings.

claim: The alternative conformations observed in TtsA and related structures may represent functionally relevant conformational states serendipitously captured in the crystal that are perhaps associated with substrate release after catalysis.
source: Although the significance of the observed alternative conformations is unclear, it is tempting to hypothesize that they may represent functionally relevant conformational states serendipitously captured in the crystal that are perhaps associated with substrate release after catalysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is speculation based on the structural data.

claim: This study provides major insight into the mechanisms of substrate specificity exhibited by a unique bacterial muramidase associated with the secretion of typhoid toxin.
source: In summary, using a multidisciplinary approach we have provided major insight into the mechanisms of substrate specificity exhibited by a unique bacterial muramidase associated with the secretion of typhoid toxin, a major virulence factor of the human pathogen S. Typhi.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the overall findings of the study.

claim: These studies may provide the bases for the potential development of anti-toxin strategies.
source: These studies may therefore provide the bases for the potential development of anti-toxin strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is speculation about potential applications of the findings.
